analysis.one_liner: Lets patients in HMO and employer health plans appeal denied care to an independent reviewer and sue when plans refuse to comply.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 40 Senate cosponsors from both parties, but was referred to the health committee on the day it was introduced in February 2001 and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set nationwide rules for managed care and employer health plans. Patients denied care would get strict deadlines for decisions, a guaranteed appeal outside the insurance company with the power to force coverage, emergency care without pre-approval, direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians, and new ways to hold plans accountable in court. It never came up for a vote; it sat in committee until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans and employer-sponsored health coverage. The bill would have required plans to make coverage decisions on fixed timelines (with 72-hour answers in emergencies), banned staff bonuses that reward denying claims, guaranteed coverage of emergency room care at in-network cost-sharing, let patients see OB-GYNs and pediatricians without gatekeeper referrals, covered approved clinical trials and minimum hospital stays after mastectomies, and given every patient whose care was denied an independent outside review whose decision binds the plan — plus civil remedies when plans refuse to comply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in HMO and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Every denial of care would be subject to an independent external review by a qualified outside entity, with the reviewer's decision binding on the plan and coverage authorized if the denial is reversed.

Plans would face firm deadlines: prior authorization within 14 days (28 days maximum), 72 hours when delay would jeopardize life or health, and written denial notices explaining the reasons in plain language.
Plans could not pay reviewers or staff in ways that encourage denials of claims, and could not interfere with doctor-patient communication about treatment options.

Emergency care would be covered without prior authorization and without penalty for using a non-network hospital or doctor, and patients would get direct access to OB-GYN, pediatric, and obstetrical care without referral.
Coverage would be required for approved clinical trials and for a minimum hospital stay after a mastectomy and lymph node dissection for breast cancer treatment.

Title III would amend ERISA to create civil remedies, letting patients in employer plans sue when plans fail to provide court-ordered coverage, with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per day and a $10,000 penalty paid to the patient for failing to follow a review determination.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance issuers and the employers and plan sponsors behind group health plans. They would bear the cost of running compliant utilization-review programs, paying for external reviews, reimbursing patients for out-of-network care obtained after a favorable review, and potential civil liability. Patients choosing the new point-of-service option would pay any additional premium themselves under the bill's terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans

drawbacks.text: The compliance and review machinery would cost plans real money, and those costs flow into premiums paid by employers and workers — a trade-off an honest supporter has to acknowledge, since tighter review standards and binding outside reviews generally increase what plans must cover.

The outside review only reaches medical-necessity, experimental-treatment, and medical-fact denials; a plan's exclusions and cost-sharing design decisions are expressly screened out of independent medical review, so the strongest patient protection still has limits.

The new right to sue under ERISA could increase litigation, which business and insurer critics argued would raise premiums and push some employers to stop offering coverage altogether; this concern drove the fight that ultimately sank the broader legislation.

Under the consumer choice option, enrollees who want to go outside their plan's network would bear any additional premium and cost-sharing themselves, so wider choice comes at the patient's own expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing denied or delayed care, the benefits are direct and concrete: binding independent review, guaranteed emergency coverage, and real consequences for plans that stonewall. The costs — higher premiums from compliance and liability exposure, and choice options patients pay for themselves — are real but diffuse. The main design limitation is that outside review cannot reach plan exclusions, only medical judgments. On balance this was a strong consumer-protection bill whose costs fell on a concentrated industry and its plan sponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never came up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the Bipartisan Patient Protection Act of 2001 on February 7, 2001, with Democratic senators including Edward Kennedy and John Edwards as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Forty senators cosponsored the bill — 38 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and no further action was ever taken on it in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans came out ahead: without the bill, they kept sole control over appeals of their own coverage denials, faced no binding outside review, no deadlines enforced by penalties, and no new private right of action for patients in employer plans. The bipartisan Senate consensus behind the measure produced no change in the rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Managed care insurers, which avoided new review and liability

for.name: 2 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republicans to do so.

for.name: American Medical Association
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed for a strong patients' bill of rights including accountability provisions during the 2001 debate.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.what_they_did: Fought the patients' bill of rights, especially the right to sue plans and binding external review, through lobbying and advertising during the 2001 debate.

against.name: George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the right-to-sue provisions of the patients' bill of rights and threatened to veto the broader legislation, pressuring Congress toward narrower liability rules.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 7, 2001 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 38 of 49 Senate Democrats and 2 of 49 Senate Republicans, with a Republican senator as lead sponsor — broad bipartisan support on paper, though the industry and White House resistance that shaped the outcome was Republican-aligned.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would have taken away their unilateral control over coverage denials, imposed binding independent review and hard deadlines enforced by daily penalties, and created a right to sue. Their business interest in controlling and limiting claim payouts ran directly against patients' interest in getting approved care.

ERISA amendments would have exposed employers and plan sponsors to new civil liability and compliance costs for the health coverage they offer workers. The cost to them came alongside enforceable protections for their own employees.
The bill would have required every denial eligible for review to go through certified outside entities paid by the plans, creating a large new market for independent review services.

Timely-payment requirements, guaranteed emergency and specialist coverage, and an end to plan interference with doctor-patient communication would have sped reimbursement and restored clinical discretion to providers.
